assertions_intent: Each eval targets a behavior the AX standards demand and a no-skill baseline plausibly gets wrong: verifying doc claims by execution instead of trusting them, shrinking agent docs via the every-line litmus instead of accreting, ask-or-mark instead of fabricating unknowns, keeping a small request small instead of escalating it into artifact-scale rework, and landing a new fact in a single source with a projection instead of syncing drifted instruction-file copies. Prompts state the user's situation in their own words and never name the skill's standards, phases, or vocabulary (no 'litmus', 'verify by execution', 'placeholder', 'projection'), so a passing run had to bring the method itself. Fixtures are self-contained projects that run offline: retrofit-cli is a working Node CLI whose README cites a nonexistent test script and a dead docs link; bloated-agents is a working Python project with a generated ~250-line AGENTS.md containing platitudes, README duplication, linter-enforced style rules, two genuinely broken commands (a make target that does not exist, a pip install for a requirements.txt that does not exist) plus a pytest instruction that happens to work (the tests are unittest-style, which pytest collects) but bypasses the Makefile entry point, and three genuine buried rules that must survive; drifted-agents is a working Python release-notes tool whose AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are drifted near-copies (each carries one load-bearing rule the other lacks), whose README cites a renamed script, and whose AGENTS.md points at a docs file that does not exist — the consult eval asks it for one small docs addition that must reach two different agent tools, grading whether the addition lands in a single source with the copy turned into a projection rather than being synced into both files. The runner copies each fixture directory into the run workspace and rewrites the path in the prompt so agents can modify their copy; greenfield runs get an empty project directory, and every run is told the user is unavailable and to record open questions rather than invent facts. Assertion tags record the outcome of the most recent measurement, and nothing else — no iteration numbers, no pending-measurement state, no note of how an assertion got its current wording. [discriminating] = with_skill passed and the baseline failed; [regression] = both configs passed, so the behavior is locked in and must not break; [reversed] = the baseline passed and with_skill failed, marking an active defect in the skill; [unmet] = both configs failed, so the bar is one neither clears yet. Re-derive the tags from each run's grading rather than editing them by hand; the narrative of what changed between runs belongs in that iteration's REPORT.md.

evals.name: retrofit-verify
evals.prompt: We're starting to let coding agents (Claude Code mostly, some teammates use Copilot) loose on our little CSV table tool, and the results have been hit and miss — last week an agent guessed how to run things, invented a test command, and declared victory without the tests ever running. The project lives in evals/files/retrofit-cli/. Can you make the repo properly agent-ready? Set up whatever instruction files and checks a coding agent needs to work reliably here.
evals.expected_output: Audit-then-generate, not generate-from-vibes. Evidence that the project's commands were actually executed (npm test, npm run lint, a CLI invocation — with captured output), and the README's two lies surfaced as explicit findings: `npm run test:unit` does not exist (real command: `npm test`) and `docs/usage.md` does not exist. A hand-written-quality AGENTS.md well under 150 lines whose command section contains only verified commands (including a single-test form) and which does not duplicate the README; a CLAUDE.md projection that imports AGENTS.md (Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md directly); boundaries/definition-of-done grounded in the real repo; anything unknowable from the repo marked as an open question rather than invented; a prioritized roadmap for what was deferred. Because the prompt names Copilot users, other-tool projection follows the pointer rule: a .github/copilot-instructions.md whose content is a one-line pointer to AGENTS.md, never a copied body. If the definition of done includes change-coupling rules (e.g. bugfix → regression test), they are marked '(to be confirmed)' — the fixture copy carries no git history to confirm them — rather than stated as team fact. The delivered docs are internally consistent with the session's own work: nothing the docs claim is contradicted by a file the session itself created or deleted, and any check or command the session installed is reachable from the docs and described at no more than its proven scope — never advertised as covering files it was not demonstrated to check.
assertions: commands-executed-with-evidence [unmet]: every command the generated agent docs list was actually executed during the session with captured output; documenting a command that was never run fails this even if the command happens to work.

stale-readme-claims-surfaced-and-fixed [regression]: both README lies are explicitly reported as findings — `npm run test:unit` does not exist (real command: npm test) and `docs/usage.md` does not exist — and the README itself is corrected so the dead references are gone from the working copy.

agents-md-verified-commands-only [discriminating]: the generated AGENTS.md commands section lists only commands that actually work in this repo (npm test, npm run lint, node src/cli.js ..., an optional single-test form) and does not carry over `npm run test:unit` or invent new commands.
single-test-command-documented [discriminating]: the generated agent docs document how to run a single test file (e.g. `node --test test/parse.test.js`), not only the full suite.

claude-md-projection [discriminating]: a CLAUDE.md exists whose content imports or points at AGENTS.md (e.g. `@AGENTS.md`) instead of duplicating it or standing alone, because Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md directly and other tools do not read CLAUDE.md.

copilot-projection-pointer-not-copy [unmet]: because the prompt says teammates use Copilot, an instruction file for Copilot exists (.github/copilot-instructions.md) whose content is a one-line pointer or import to AGENTS.md (e.g. 'Read AGENTS.md in the project root.'), not a copy of AGENTS.md content — a duplicated body fails even with a do-not-edit header.
root-map-not-manual [discriminating]: AGENTS.md is at most 150 lines, does not restate README content (project pitch, feature list, zero-install notes), and contains no full directory tree.

no-fabricated-facts [reversed]: the generated docs state no facts the repo cannot support — no invented CI systems, deploy processes, style rules, or team conventions, and no small unverified generalizations either (e.g. claiming a test file exists per src module when one module has none); claims about tooling the session itself installed count the same way (advertising a new check as covering files it was never proven to cover fails); anything unknowable from the repo is marked as an open question rather than asserted.

docs-consistent-with-session-changes [regression]: the delivered instruction files are consistent with the session's own changes — no claim contradicted by a file the session itself created or deleted (e.g. stating there is no CI configuration alongside a workflow file the session just added, or referencing README content the session already removed).

remediation-roadmap-delivered [regression]: the run delivers a prioritized list of deferred improvements (a roadmap) in summary.md, the final response, or a generated doc, with at least one item naming a concrete file, command, or decision in this repo — a list of only generic ecosystem advice ('add CI', 'improve test coverage') does not count — rather than presenting the session's output as complete and final.

evals.name: improve-shrink
evals.prompt: A teammate had some AI tool generate the AGENTS.md in evals/files/bloated-agents/ a few months ago. I don't trust it anymore: it's enormous, agents seem to ignore half of it, and I suspect parts are plain wrong. Please review our agent docs against current AX best practices and fix them up — I want something that actually helps agents instead of drowning them.
evals.expected_output: The AGENTS.md shrinks to a small fraction of its 250+ lines, with reasoning tied to whether each removed line would have prevented a real mistake: platitudes, the README-duplicating overview, the full file tree, and the style rules already enforced by the ruff config in pyproject.toml all go. The broken commands are caught by actually running them — `make check` has no target and `pip install -r requirements.txt` fails (there is no requirements.txt) — and the rewrite cites the verified `make test`. The AGENTS.md's pytest instruction is a different trap: the tests are unittest-style, so pytest happens to collect and pass them, but it bypasses the Makefile entry point — the rewrite keeps the Makefile targets as the single documented command surface instead of retaining or introducing parallel raw invocations. The three genuine project rules survive: never hand-edit shiftplan/data/holidays.json (regenerate with make fixtures), the naive-datetime/no-tzinfo policy, and PAY_MULTIPLIERS in shiftplan/payroll.py as the single source for rate factors. A CLAUDE.md projection exists after the rewrite, application code is untouched, and no tool caches or build artifacts are left in the delivered copy.
assertions: substantially-shorter [regression]: the rewritten AGENTS.md is at most half the original's 256 lines (programmatically checkable via wc -l).

platitudes-and-duplication-removed [regression]: the generic best-practices content (the bare don't-list, write-clean-code style advice, Arrange-Act-Assert guidance) and the full directory tree are gone, and no README paragraph survives wholesale — a project-identity snapshot of at most 3 source lines that overlaps the README is acceptable; verbatim reproduction beyond that is not.

linter-enforced-style-removed [unmet]: prose style rules already enforced by the ruff configuration in pyproject.toml no longer appear in the rewritten docs — restating any enforced value fails even when phrased as a pointer ('line length 100, per ruff config'), while a pointer naming only the tool and config location ('style is enforced by ruff — see pyproject.toml') passes.

broken-commands-proven-by-execution [unmet]: the broken commands were proven broken by actually running them or their direct equivalents in-session (`make check` and `pip install -r requirements.txt` failing, `make test` or its underlying unittest invocation succeeding — execution evidence in the transcript or summary), not declared broken from file reads alone.

stale-commands-gone-from-docs [regression]: the rewritten docs no longer instruct using `make check` or `pip install -r requirements.txt` (an explicit warning such as 'there is no requirements.txt' is acceptable) and cite the verified `make test`.

task-runner-surface-consistent [regression]: the rewritten docs keep the Makefile as the command surface — test and fixture commands are cited as `make test` / `make fixtures`, not replaced with their raw underlying invocations — and the delivered copy ends with one documented entry point per verb: no surviving doc contradicts another about how to run tests (README.md's `make test` must still hold), and keeping pytest alongside `make test` as a second undifferentiated entry point also fails.

genuine-rules-retained [regression]: all three load-bearing project rules survive the rewrite: (1) never hand-edit shiftplan/data/holidays.json — regenerate with make fixtures; (2) datetimes stay naive / no tzinfo in scheduler or payroll code; (3) PAY_MULTIPLIERS in shiftplan/payroll.py is the single source for rate factors.
claude-md-projection [discriminating]: after the rewrite a CLAUDE.md exists that imports or points at AGENTS.md rather than duplicating it.

litmus-reasoning-explained [regression]: the run's delivered reasoning — in summary.md, the final response, or a delivered doc — justifies removals by whether a line would prevent a real agent mistake or duplicates already-enforced or already-documented content, not merely 'made it shorter'.

no-new-false-claims [regression]: the rewrite introduces no new inaccurate or environment-coupled claims into the durable docs (e.g. 'ruff is not installed in this environment' — true only of the sandbox that ran the audit — must not land in AGENTS.md as a project fact); pointers to content that does not exist count ('see the open question below' with no such content below).

application-code-untouched [regression]: shiftplan/ source code, tests/, and shiftplan/data/ fixtures are unchanged from the fixture copy — new docs-tooling files (e.g. a docs-check script or Makefile target) are acceptable, edits to application code or tests are not.
working-copy-clean [discriminating]: the delivered copy contains no stray tool caches or build artifacts introduced by the session (.ruff_cache/, .pytest_cache/, __pycache__/, or similar).

evals.name: greenfield-interview
evals.prompt: I'm about to start a brand-new project and I want it set up for agent-first development from day one — the plan is that coding agents write most of the code and my colleague and I mostly review. What I know so far: it's an internal tool for the ops team at our logistics company to plan driver shifts across our three depots, the dispatchers will use it in the browser, and the two of us are comfortable in TypeScript. Nothing exists yet, no repo, no code. Set up the foundations for me.
evals.expected_output: Interview-first, fabricate-nothing. The run either asks the user targeted questions or — where no answer is available — records explicit '(to be confirmed)' open questions for product/technical facts it cannot know (data store, hosting, auth, data-privacy constraints, integrations); it does not invent a database, cloud provider, or compliance stance, and it does not poll the user about the AX layer's own design ('would you like an ARCHITECTURE.md?', 'how long should AGENTS.md be?' — those follow from convention). Stack and topology recommendations are justified by affordances: TypeScript strict mode as a free sensor, a constraining mainstream framework, fast test tooling, module boundaries expressible as import rules. It delivers a day-one AX layer around a scaffold: root AGENTS.md map + CLAUDE.md projection, a task-runner command surface, initial sensors wired (typecheck, lint, fast tests), and a docs nucleus with ADRs recording the stack/topology decisions and open questions. ADRs carry their lifecycle status in structured, machine-readable form (YAML frontmatter status: proposed/accepted), and the definition of done states what must accompany each kind of change (e.g. a test with every feature or bugfix) as labeled defaults or open questions — with the user unavailable, couplings cannot be confirmed as team policy. It does not generate application features — the ceiling is a smoke-tested placeholder route and an empty labeled schema stub, because the verification loop is proven by sensors firing, not by a working feature. The delivered artifacts are internally consistent with the session's own work: no doc or ADR claim contradicted by a file the session itself created, and no question the run filed as open silently answered by its own implementation.
assertions: no-fabricated-product-facts [discriminating]: the run invents no product or infrastructure facts beyond the prompt — no chosen database, cloud provider, auth provider, or compliance stance stated as fact, and no invented product color either: no names for the three depots, no predecessor-system backstory, no rule or statement attributed to the user that the prompt does not contain; each genuine unknown appears as a question to the user or an explicit open/to-be-confirmed item (a recommended default clearly labeled as a default is acceptable).

questions-target-facts-not-ax-design [regression]: all questions and open items target product or technical facts (data store, hosting, auth, integrations, data rules, quality bars); none ask the user to design the agent setup itself (e.g. 'would you like an ARCHITECTURE.md?', 'should I create ADRs?', 'how long should AGENTS.md be?').

affordance-justified-stack [discriminating]: stack and topology recommendations are justified by properties that help agents work reliably (static typing / TypeScript strict as machine verification, a constraining mainstream framework, fast test/build feedback, module boundaries enforceable via imports) — not just popularity or personal preference.

day-one-root-map [discriminating]: the created scaffold includes a root AGENTS.md map and a CLAUDE.md that imports/points at it — both must exist, and the AGENTS.md carries verified project-specific content (this project's actual commands, layout, or constraints); a generator-emitted boilerplate pair left as scaffolded (e.g. what create-next-app emits) fails, as does a standalone AGENTS.md with no CLAUDE.md or the reverse.
day-one-command-surface [regression]: the scaffold has a task-runner command surface (package scripts or Makefile) with initial verification wiring for typecheck, lint, and test.
day-one-docs-nucleus [discriminating]: the scaffold includes a docs nucleus — an ARCHITECTURE.md and/or decision records — as repo artifacts, not only as prose in the summary or final response.

decisions-recorded-durably [discriminating]: each major stack/topology choice is recorded as an actual decision record — with rationale and a lifecycle status (proposed/accepted) in structured, machine-readable form such as YAML frontmatter, not only free prose — and the open questions are filed in a repo artifact; a bare normative 'Stack' section without rationale or status does not count.

no-application-features [discriminating]: no shift-planning business logic is implemented — no rota or scheduling algorithms (domain logic with tests counts even when framed as proving the loop), no seeded domain data (rows for the three depots count), no working dispatcher UI, and no vertical slice of endpoint plus screen plus data; the ceiling is a smoke-tested placeholder route and an empty, clearly-labeled schema or model stub (e.g. a Depot placeholder in a scaffold schema).

docs-consistent-with-session-work [unmet]: the delivered artifacts are internally consistent with the session's own work — no doc or ADR claim contradicted by a file the session itself created (e.g. 'no CI wiring exists yet' alongside a workflow file added in the same session, or a package name contradicting package.json), and no question the run itself filed as open is silently answered by its own implementation in the same session.

scaffold-proven-by-execution [discriminating]: the scaffold's verification loop was proven green by execution in the delivered state — install proven against the delivered lockfile (a fresh or frozen-lockfile install, not a warm store's 'Already up to date'), typecheck/lint/test actually run with captured output — not merely written into config files.

evals.name: consult-single-source
evals.prompt: Quick one, hopefully. In evals/files/drifted-agents/ we have both an AGENTS.md and a CLAUDE.md — I'm on Claude Code, my teammate uses Codex, and at some point one of those files got copied from the other; both have picked up their own edits since. What I actually need: our agent docs say nothing about how release notes work here. CHANGELOG.md is assembled from the little fragment files in changes/, and any agent that changes user-facing behavior is supposed to add a fragment and rebuild the changelog — but nothing tells them that. Can you add that workflow to the agent instructions? Make sure it lands in a way that my Claude Code sessions and my teammate's Codex sessions both actually pick up.
evals.expected_output: A small request gets a single-source answer. The trap is the file pair: Claude Code reads only CLAUDE.md while Codex reads AGENTS.md natively, so the obvious move — writing the new workflow into both drifted copies to 'make sure both tools see it' — entrenches the fork. The right shape: the workflow (add a one-line changes/<issue>-<slug>.md fragment, rebuild with the verified `make changelog`) lands once in AGENTS.md as the source, and CLAUDE.md becomes a projection that imports or points at AGENTS.md — which is exactly how both tools pick it up. The consolidation is lossless: the tests-use-temp-dirs rule (previously AGENTS.md-only) and the __version__-single-source rule (previously CLAUDE.md-only) both survive. The rebuild command is proven by actually running it — README's `python3 scripts/gen_changelog.py` is stale (the script is scripts/build_changelog.py, targeted by `make changelog`), so paraphrasing prose without execution documents a dead command. The run stays consult-sized: no audit inventory, interview, remediation roadmap, or readiness score, and surviving content is not rewritten wholesale; adjacent defects met on the way (the stale README command, the dead docs/RELEASING.md pointer) are surfaced as findings or minimal fixes, with any fuller review offered rather than launched.
assertions: new-fact-single-source [discriminating]: the release-notes workflow is added to exactly one durable source — AGENTS.md — and by session end CLAUDE.md imports or points at AGENTS.md (e.g. a pure `@AGENTS.md` import, optionally with genuinely Claude-specific notes below it) instead of remaining a parallel copy; writing the new workflow into both files to keep the copies in sync, writing it only into CLAUDE.md, or deleting CLAUDE.md outright all fail.

consolidation-lossless [discriminating]: both facts that existed in only one of the two files are reachable from both tools' entry points after the change — tests build fragments in temp directories rather than touching the repo's changes/ (previously AGENTS.md-only) and __version__ in relnotes/__init__.py as the only place the version lives (previously CLAUDE.md-only) each end up in AGENTS.md or somewhere it points, with CLAUDE.md importing or pointing at AGENTS.md so Claude Code sessions see them too; dropping either fact fails, and leaving the two files as separate drifted copies also fails — each fact then stays invisible to one of the two tools.

rebuild-command-executed [discriminating]: the rebuild harness (make changelog or python3 scripts/build_changelog.py) was actually executed during the session with captured output; writing the command into the docs without having run it fails even when the command cited is correct.

rebuild-command-cited-correctly [regression]: the documented rebuild instruction cites the real harness (make changelog or python3 scripts/build_changelog.py), not README's stale `python3 scripts/gen_changelog.py`.

edit-stays-consult-sized [regression]: beyond the requested addition, the two-file consolidation, and at most minimal fixes to stale references met along the way, nothing is restructured — no audit inventory, interview, remediation roadmap, or readiness score is produced, and the surviving AGENTS.md content is not rewritten wholesale.

adjacent-defects-surfaced-with-offer [regression]: at least one defect discovered en route — the stale rebuild command in README.md or the dead docs/RELEASING.md reference in AGENTS.md — is explicitly surfaced (in summary.md, the final response, or a delivered doc) or minimally fixed, and deeper follow-up work (a fuller docs review, wiring checks) is offered in any of those channels rather than launched; staying silent about both defects fails.
